2185-maruja:
In old California, a proud young woman named Maruja stands at the center of family pride, land, and love. Bret Harte draws on the world of Spanish ranchos, where old families guard their names and their estates against a changing time. The novel moves between grand houses, ranch work, and the social rules that bind its people.

Maruja herself is headstrong and warm, and her choices drive the story as suitors, relatives, and rivals press their claims. Harte fills the scenes with local color and sharp dialogue, but the plot stays close to one woman's heart and honor. It is a romance of California's past, told with affection for its people and its landscape.
22670-jack-wright-and-his-electric-stage:
Jack Wright and His Electric Stage, or Leagued Against the James Boys, is a dime novel of the famous boy inventor Jack Wright and his marvelous electric stagecoach. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. The Jack Wright stories, printed in cheap weeklies, pitted the young inventor's machines against the West's most famous outlaws.

In the sample, the hunters plan an ambush at a curve where timber, brush, and rocks jut close to the road. There the train must slacken speed, and the ground will hide their movements from the sheriff's view. Wheels, wires, and gunplay mix freely in this kind of tale. The book is pure period pulp: swift, improbable, and proud of it, built for boys with a nickel and an afternoon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beja:
Beja is a Portuguese diocese, suffragan of Evora, created in 1770 with 175,000 Catholics, 115 parishes, and 197 churches. Its city, capital of Baixo Alemtejo, is thought to be Rome's Pax Julia, still ringed by partly medieval-restored Roman walls. Affonso Henriques took it from the Moors in 1162, and it stands on a high hill amid fertile valleys of cereals, oil, and wine.

Its castle, built by King Dom Diniz, is a square mass 120 feet high, Portugal's finest surviving medieval architecture. From its top the whole Alemtejo and the Cintra mountains can be seen, and its walls bear hieroglyphics. An early episcopal city, it lost that dignity under the Moors, and its cathedral is now too modernized to date. The city holds about 8,000 people and ranks richest in Roman remains after Evora.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-de-:
Francisco de Rioja, born at Seville in 1583 and dead at Madrid in 1659, was a Spanish poet and canon of Seville cathedral who also served the Supreme Inquisition. His poems, Quintana judged, were the first attempts at descriptive poetry in Castilian, original in style, beautifully thought, refined in taste, and versified in harmony with their themes. Menendez y Pelayo ranked his odes to summer, tranquillity, constancy, riches, and poverty just after the lyrics of Fray Luis de Leon among Castilian moral odes.

Two famous poems long given to Rioja are not his. The ode on the ruins of Italy belongs to Rodrigo Caro, and the moral epistle probably to Francisco de Andrada. Yet stripped of those gems he remains highly esteemed by Spanish scholars. His best edition is Barrera's of 1867, with additions in 1872, and his finest poems appear in Rivadeneira's library of Spanish authors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-par:
Francisco Pareja, probably born at Aunon in the diocese of Toledo and dead in Mexico on 25 January 1628. He was a Franciscan missionary who published the first books in an Indian language within the present United States. Sent to Florida with eleven other Franciscans, he arrived at St. Augustine in 1593 or early 1594 and laboured among the peoples of the peninsula, notably at San Juan on the coast. He became guardian of the monastery of the Immaculate Conception at St. Augustine, later styled custos before the custody became a province in 1613.

Joining the province of the Holy Gospel in Mexico, he gave the Timuquanan language its first printed literature. It began with a catechism in Spanish and Timuquanan in 1612, a brief exposition of Christian doctrine the same year, a confessional in both languages in 1613. A grammar of Timuquanan followed in 1614, another catechism in 1617, and a catechism and examination for communicants in 1627.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-loja:
Loja is a diocese in south-west Ecuador, suffragan of Quito, spanning most of Loja and El Oro provinces between the Andes and the Pacific. Its city, founded about 1546 to guard the royal road from Quito to Peru, ranks among the oldest towns in the land.

Loja hosted Ecuador's first provincial council in 1580, and there a Spanish soldier first learned the fever-curing bark of cinchona, source of quinine, after it cured the vicereine of Peru. Quakes and Indian raids battered the town, and a bishopric rose only in 1866. Its bishops, Checa, Riofrio, and the exiled Masia, anchor the later story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tunja:
A diocese established in 1880 as a suffragan of Bogotá, covering the Department of Boyacá in Colombia, with 400,000 Catholics, 145 priests, 153 parishes and 159 churches and chapels in 1911. Its see city, Tunja, was called Hunza before the Spaniards came and housed the zaque, sovereign of the Muisca Indians.

Captain Gonzalo Suárez Rondón founded the city on 6 August 1538 by order of the conqueror Quesada, and Charles V granted it city rank in 1681. The wealth of its early founders still shows in coats-of-arms carved over stone mansion entrances, and the department runs over 200 primary schools with about 15,000 pupils of both sexes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincenzo-da-f:
Vincenzo da Filicaja was a Florentine lyric poet who lived from 1642 to 1707. Trained at Pisa for law, which he practised, he also pursued philosophy, literature, and music, joined the Accademia della Crusca and the Arcadia on returning to Florence. Enjoyed the patronage of Christina, ex-Queen of Sweden, whose purse eased his family burdens.

A lawyer and magistrate of integrity who never grew wealthy, he was acknowledged by those in power and appointed to posts of great trust: senator under Grand Duke Cosimo III. Governor of Volterra in 1696 and Pisa in 1700, then secretary of the draws at Florence. An ardent Catholic, he often voiced religious feeling in lyrics notably free, for their age, from Marinist bombast, exaggeration. Obscurity, above all in odes on Sobieski's raising of Vienna's siege in 1683 and sonnets bewailing Italy's woes.
maruja:
Bret Harte set his novel Maruja on the high road to San Jose. Dawn breaks over wheat and oat fields in the first scene. A coyote and a young tramp cross the plain, half a mile apart.

Man and beast share a lazy, stray look in Harte's close prose. The tramp turns off the road to dodge the dogs of a farm. He rests in a hollow of wild clover, with bread crusts and time to waste. Harte lingers on light, dust, and scent as the day warms. The slow start builds the old California world the title figure rules.
podcast-joerogan-1OnBVqeW5JA:
Magician Penn Jillette joins Joe Rogan for episode 1343 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Jillette is the tall, loud half of Penn and Teller and a famed libertarian voice. His talks mix tricks, tales, and hard views on state power.

Jillette and Rogan talk shop on stage craft, fame, and the right to say what you please. He tells tales from a life in Vegas and on the road with a silent partner. Rogan meets him as a fellow foe of bans and scolds. Listeners get a big voice at ease. The library keeps the episode as a record of his visit.
podcast-joerogan-__Czlg1xLJA:
Fauci, gain-of-function research, and Wuhan lab funding form the core of a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. Rogan works through the fight over whether U.S. money, routed through grants, supported risky virus work in China. The argument sits at the center of the COVID origins war.

He lays out the claims and counter-claims: what gain-of-function means, what Dr. Fauci told Congress, and what the documents show. The segment is a dated but sharp record of the debate, useful for readers who want the critics' case assembled in one place, in the host's own combative order.
podcast-tuckercarlson-oZTmlsfH0JA:
Tucker Carlson and Chris Cuomo face off in a debate that roams across the day's loudest fights. The title names the JFK and Epstein files, DOGE, Joe Rogan, NATO, and fights over trans policy and DEI. Cuomo is a news host from the other side of the dial.

The two men spar over what the sealed files hide and what the new team in power has done. They clash on war, speech, and who the press serves. The tone stays sharp but civil. Listeners get a rare cross-line debate in full. The library holds it as a record of two hosts in open dispute.
